The short answer is no. A physical book and a library ebook may both be loans, but they don't give the lender the same kind of power. When you return a paper book, you hand back the object and the library can lend that object again. When your ebook vanishes because the publisher withdrew it, the library hasn't recovered an object from you; your access has been switched off.

That distinction matters. You paid attention, waited your turn, and used the loan under the terms offered. You didn't break the book, keep it past the due date, or sneak around a lock. The thing you borrowed simply stopped being available. If a bookseller could enter your house and remove a print book from the shelf after the sale, we'd call that theft, not a normal return. A digital loan isn't a sale, but the comparison exposes the missing piece: possession and permission aren't the same thing.

I think the library should tell readers plainly when a title can be revoked, and I am wary of contracts that make disappearance sound like routine administration. (The legal wording may be complicated.) The practical fact is simple: you had access, and then you didn't.

Should libraries accept this as inevitable? No. They can demand clearer terms, preserve usable copies when licensing permits, and explain what happens before borrowing. A borrower can also ask whether a replacement edition or another format exists, though that remedy leaves the particular loan gone.

We need rules that treat digital lending as a public service, not as a vending machine whose owner can reach through the screen whenever it suits them. (That image is deliberately blunt.) A vanished file is more than a returned book. It is the loss of temporary control that made the loan meaningful. The difference is small only if we ignore the reader standing on the other side of it.
